newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - GA profits sink, but outlook positive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - GA profits sink, but outlook positive.

text.p: Scottish-based insurer General Accident Plc, hurt by severe weather losses in the United States, on Tuesday reported a fall in profits but said improved life results had limited the damage.

GA suffered an 11 percent or 40 million pounds ($66.11 million) decline in nine-month operating profits to 311 million pounds -- in line with analysts' forecasts. This included losses of 58 million mainly due to the effects of winter weather in the U.S. earlier this year.
But this masked a 23 percent year-on-year rise in third quarter operating profits to 117 million pounds, helped by a sharp increase in sales of personal pensions in Britain.
In addition, the non-life worldwide underwriting deficit deteriorated by only three million pounds to 56 million during this period -- a more modest slide than earlier in the year.

"The positive underlying performance in all our major business units worldwide which we reported at the half year has continued during the third quarter and we would expect this trend to be maintained," said group chief executive Bob Scott.

Pension sales in Britain rose to 63.7 million pounds from 22.2 million in the third quarter and now account for nearly half of GA Life's new business. Group long-term business profits for the first nine months rose to 77 million from 53 million.
The integration of Provident Mutual, which GA bought in January, is "largely complete" and the business contributed 11 million pounds net of reorganisation costs to group profits.

GA had thought a projected 25 million pounds full year contribution from Provident Mutual would be eaten up by the restructuring charges, but analysts now expect the acquisition to contribute well over 30 million pounds to the full year.
However, fierce competition in British personal motor insurance is keeping profits there under pressure and GA has not increased rates since a selective six percent hike in June.
GA also revealed that it was selling several small non-core businesses overseas as part of efforts to focus resources on markets where it had "advantages of scale and synergy".
Scott said in an interview with Reuters that GA planned to sell its business in Puerto Rico by the end of this year as part of efforts to refocus the group's portfolio.
He said GA had received offers for the Caribbean-based life and general insurance business, which earns around $100 million in premium income and underwrites mainly hurricane risks.

Puerto Rico experienced a sharp deterioration in performance last year, when the cost of Hurricane Marilyn affected results badly. The sale of this division would follow the disposal of small businesses in the U.S. and Kenya during the third quarter.

But despite these moves and restructuring of the group's business in Britain, some analysts questioned whether GA can compete effectively in the longer term with major insurers like France's Axa and UAP, which on Tuesday announced plans to merge creating a world insurance giant.
The alliance between Europe's second and third biggest insurers follows the 5.4 billion pounds merger of British composites Royal Insurance and Sun Alliance in July.

"You either have to be big or small and the middle-sized guys get squeezed out. That's the big issue that needs to be addressed and GA is rapidly becoming a medium-sized player," said insurance analyst David Hudson at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
Scott does not think GA needs to merge with another large insurer to compete effectively. The group has already cut costs following a restructuring programme in the early 1990s.

It is still looking for an acquisition in France similar to the small commercial lines business it bought in Germany this year, but in the highly competitive UK market GA is more likely to try and achieve growth organically where possible.
